question: Determine the values of $a$ and $b$ for which the function $$f(x)=\begin{cases}ax+b, & x\leq2\\ x^2-2x+5, & x>2\end{cases}$$ is differentiable at $x=2$, giving complete justification for the required values.
explanation:
Continuity Requirement
A function differentiable at a point must also be continuous at that point. Hence, for differentiability at $x=2$, the function must first satisfy the condition of continuity there.

Using the first branch, $$f(2)=2a+b.$$ The right-hand limit is obtained from the second branch: $$\lim_{x\to2^+}f(x)=2^2-2(2)+5=5.$$ Therefore, continuity at $x=2$ requires $$2a+b=5.$$

Differentiability Requirement
The left-hand derivative and right-hand derivative at $x=2$ must be finite and equal. For $x<2$, $f(x)=ax+b$, so its derivative is $a$. Hence, $$f'_-(2)=a.$$ For $x>2$, $$f(x)=x^2-2x+5,$$ so $$f'(x)=2x-2.$$ Therefore, $$f'_+(2)=2(2)-2=2.$$ Differentiability requires $$f'_-(2)=f'_+(2),$$ giving $$a=2.$$

Substituting $a=2$ in $2a+b=5$, we get $$4+b=5,$$ and hence $$b=1.$$

Verification
For $a=2$ and $b=1$, $$f(2)=2(2)+1=5,$$ which agrees with the right-hand limit. Also, $$f'_-(2)=2=f'_+(2).$$

Final Result
Hence the function is differentiable at $x=2$ precisely when $$a=2,\qquad b=1.$$
